Senior Secured Credit  Agreement, (d) the failure to perform any other provision of the Senior Secured  Credit Agreement (other than those set forth in (b) above) which nonperformance  remains un-remedied for 20 days or more, (e) a default or breach under any  other agreement or instrument to which we are a party beyond any grace period  that involves the failure to pay in excess of $250,000 or causes or permits to  cause indebtedness in excess of $250,000 to become due prior to its stated  maturity, (f) any information in a borrowing base certificate or any  representation or warranty or certificate or in any written statement report,  or financial statement delivered to GECC being untrue or incorrect in any  material respect, (g) a change of control, as defined, of the Company, (h) the  occurrence of an event having a material adverse effect, (i) the initiation of  insolvency, bankruptcy or liquidation proceedings, (j) any final judgment for  the payment of money in excess of $250,000 is outstanding
against the Company  and is not within thirty days discharged, stayed or bonded pending appeal, (k)  any material provision of or lien under any document relating to the Senior  Secured Credit Agreement ceases to be valid, (l) the attachment, seizure or  levy upon of the Company&#146;s assets which continues for 30 days or more, and (m)  William Jenkins ceases to serve as the Company&#146;s chief executive officer,  unless otherwise agreed by GECC. Upon the occurrence of a default, which is  defined as any event that with the passage of time or notice or both would,  unless waived or cured, become an event of default, or event of default, the  lenders may discontinue making revolving loans and capital expenditure loans to  the Company and increase the interest rate on all loans. Upon the occurrence of  an event of default, the lenders may terminate the Senior Secured Credit  Agreement, declare all indebtedness outstanding under the Senior Secured Credit  Agreement due and payable, and exercise any of
their rights under the Senior  Secured Credit Agreement which includes the ability to foreclose on our assets.  In the event of a bankruptcy or liquidation proceeding, all borrowings under  the Senior Secured Credit Agreement are immediately due and payable.</font></div>

to an  anti-dilution adjustment for certain issuances of securities by the Company at  prices per share of common stock less than the conversion price then in effect,  in which event the conversion price is reduced to the lower price at which the  shares were issued.&#160; As a condition to  extend the maturity date of the notes in connection with the GECC refinancing  in November 2004, the Company extended the expiration date of our 6.6 million  outstanding common stock purchase warrants to December 31, 2009.</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">All of the debt and interest owed under the  subordinated secured promissory notes is subordinated to the Senior Credit  Agreement and the Second Lien Credit Agreement and cannot be repaid until all  the amounts owed pursuant to the Credit Facility have been repaid.&#160; </font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">Substantially all of the Company&#146;s  assets are pledged as collateral for the indebtedness outstanding under the  Secured Credit Agreement and the Second Lien Credit Agreement and subordinated secured promissory notes.</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman"><b>Note 11 - Common Stock Transactions and Warrants</b></font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">In October 2005, the Company initiated a series of steps undertaken for  the purpose of recapitalizing the Company through the elimination of the  substantial amount of derivative securities it has outstanding, among other  steps intended to be undertaken. These derivative securities include common  stock purchase warrants to purchase 7,076,119 shares of the Company&#146;s common  stock and $35,019,173 of principal amount and accrued interest, as of December  31, 2005, of the Company&#146;s outstanding convertible subordinated notes which, as  of that date, are convertible at a conversion price of $7.50 per share into an  aggregate of 4,669,223 shares of the Company&#146;s common stock.</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">On October 6, 2005, the Company entered into agreements with the  holders of 5,269,369 of the 7,076,119 warrants outstanding to exchange those  warrants for 1,756,456 shares of the Company&#146;s common stock. Of the 5,269,369  warrants, an aggregate of 4,075,528 are held by the SJCP and SJMB, and  1,193,841 were held by the Underbrink Family Entities, which include Mr.&nbsp;Charles  E. Underbrink. Mr.&nbsp;Underbrink is one of the Company&#146;s directors and is the  Chairman of the general partner of SJMB and, in October 2005, was the Chairman  of the general partner of SJCP. The exchange of warrants for shares of the  Company&#146;s common stock by the Underbrink Family Entities was completed on  October&nbsp;6, 2005 resulting in the issuance of 397,947 shares, and the  warrants to purchase 4,075,527 shares held by SJCP and SJMB are to be  repurchased in connection with the Company&#146;s proposed public offering.</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">On October 7, 2005, the Company commenced an offer to exchange shares  of its common stock for its remaining outstanding 1,806,750 common stock  purchase warrants. The Company offered to exchange one share of our common  stock for each three warrants. Each warrant represents the right to purchase  one share of the Company&#146;s common stock at an exercise price of $7.50 per  share. The offer to exchange shares of the Company&#146;s common stock for warrants  expired on November&nbsp;14, 2005, and the Company issued 503,167 shares of its  common stock in exchange for 1,509,500 common stock purchase warrants.</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">The agreements with SJCP, SJMB and the Underbrink Family Entities  provide that such persons will convert an aggregate of $20,277,374 of principal  and all accrued interest (which amounted to $16,734,434 through December 31,  2005) on the Company&#146;s outstanding convertible subordinated notes into shares  of our common stock and, provided the price they are to receive is not less  than $7.50 per share, sell those shares to the Company, along with their  remaining warrants, the shares issued in exchange for certain of their  warrants, the shares issued on conversion of accrued interest in November 2005  and an additional 501,748 shares held by SJMB, at the closing time of the Company&#146;s  proposed public offering. The purchase price paid by the Company for such  shares will be the price per share it receives in the public offering less  commissions and expenses of the underwriters in the offering.&#160; In addition, under the terms of a Registration
Rights Agreement, the holders of $3,041,361 principal amount and accrued  interest (as of December 31, 2005) on outstanding convertible subordinated  notes have the right to have included 405,515 shares issuable on conversion of  the principal and interest on the notes, as well as the shares of the Company&#146;s  common stock issued in exchange for their warrants, in the registration  statement relating to the Company&#146;s proposed public offering.</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">As of December 31, 2005, the Company&#146;s certificate of incorporation  permits it to issue up to 35,000,000 shares of common stock, of which 2,342,125  shares were issued and outstanding at December 31, 2005 and 1,250,415 shares  were issued and outstanding at December 31, 2004.&#160; The Company has outstanding as of December 31, 2005 and 2004  common stock purchase warrants, options and convertible debt securities entitled  to purchase or be converted into an aggregate of 8,019,484 and 13,382,167  shares, respectively, of the Company&#146;s common stock at exercise and conversion  prices ranging from $7.50 to $26.30.&#160; </font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">During 2004, the Company became obligated to issue five-year warrants  to purchase 802,856 shares of common stock to SJMB and related parties of SJMB  exercisable at $7.50 per share in connection with the extension of their  indebtedness <i>(see Note 9)</i>.&#160; These  warrants were issued in 2005.</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">During 2003, the Company issued five-year warrants to purchase 518,766  of common stock to SJMB and related parties of SJMB exercisable at $7.50 per  share in connection with the extension of their indebtedness <i>(see Note 9)</i>.</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">During 2002, the Company issued five-year warrants to purchase 250,000  shares of common stock to William L. Jenkins, President and Chief Executive  Officer exercisable at $7.50 per share pursuant to his amended employment  agreement effective January 1, 2002 and expiring December 31, 2005 and extended  in March 2005 through January 1, 2008.</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">During 2002, the Company issued five-year warrants to purchase 242,209  to SJMB and affiliates of SJMB exercisable at $7.50 per share in connection  with the extension of their indebtedness <i>(see Note 9)</i>.</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">During 2001, the Company issued to the Chairman of SJMB, L.L.C. and to  SJCP five-year warrants to purchase 70,000 and 400,000 shares, respectively, of  the Company&#146;s Common Stock at exercise prices of $7.50 per share.&#160; The warrants were issued in consideration of  guarantees extended to a lender by the Chairman of SJMB, L.L.C. and SJCP in  connection with the Company&#146;s borrowings in 2000 and the guarantees of the  Chairman of SJMB, L.L.C. and SJCP of that indebtedness.</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">The warrants issued during 2004, 2003, 2002, 2001, 2000 and 1999 are  subject to &#147;Full Ratchet&#148; anti-dilution provisions. In December of 1999, the  Company issued the 14,350,000 warrants at an exercise price of $7.50.&#160; Consequently, the anti-dilution provisions  on all warrants subject to the provision were triggered. Upon each adjustment  of the exercise price, the holder of the warrant shall thereafter is entitled  to purchase, at the exercise price resulting from the adjustment, the number of  shares of common stock obtained by multiplying the exercise price in effect  immediately prior to the adjustment by the number of shares purchasable prior  to the adjustment and dividing the product thereof by the exercise price  resulting from the adjustment. The following table summarizes information about  warrants outstanding at December 31, 2005:</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">At December 31, 2005 and 2004, the Company has available federal tax  net operating loss carryforwards (NOL&#146;s) of approximately $29,304,631 and  $35,556,000, respectively, that unless previously utilized, expire at various  dates beginning 2011 through 2024. The Company&#146;s utilization of NOL&#146;s is  subject to a number of uncertainties, including the ability to generate future  taxable income.&#160; In addition, the Company  has been subject to a number of &#147;ownership changes&#148; as defined under Internal  Revenue Code Section 382. As a result, Section 382 imposes additional  limitations on utilization of certain of the Company&#146;s NOL&#146;s.&#160; Subsequent to the Company&#146;s proposed public  offering it expects to begin paying income taxes on its taxable income.&#160;&#160; </font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">The Company is required to record a valuation allowance when it is more  likely than not that some portion or all of the deferred tax assets will not be  realized. At December 31, 2005 and 2004, the Company has recorded a valuation  allowance of $6,441,690 and $14,627,450 against the gross deferred tax asset.</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">In assessing the realizability of deferred tax assets, management  considers future reversals of existing deferred tax liabilities, projected  future taxable income exclusive of temporary differences and available tax planning  strategies.&#160; In 2005, the Company  recorded a decrease in the valuation allowance of $8.2 million.&#160; The decrease was recorded as a $3.0 million  reduction of the provision for income taxes and as a $5.2 million reduction of  the deferred tax liability and goodwill associated with the acquisition of  Bobcat (see Note 2).</font></div>

  <div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman"><b>Warrior Energy Services Corporation</b></font></div>
  <div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman"><b>Notes to Financial Statements</b></font></div>
  <div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman"><b>For the Years Ended December 31, 2005, 2004 and 2003</b></font></div>
  <div>
    <hr noshade size="1">
  </div>



</div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">Options issued to purchase 1,059,800 shares of common stock and  warrants to purchase 1,655,759 shares of common stock at prices ranging from  $7.50 to $26.30 were outstanding during 2005.&#160;  Of the 1,059,800 options outstanding during 2005, all but 500 options  are exercisable at $7.50 and all of the 1,655,759 warrants are exercisable at  $7.50. </font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">Options issued to purchase 1,059,280 shares of common stock and  warrants to purchase 6,855,118 shares of common stock at price ranging from  $7.50 to $66.30 were outstanding during 2004, but were not included in the  computation of the 2004 diluted EPS because the effect would be anti-dilutive.&#160; There were 484,720 options to purchase  common stock cancelled during 2004 that were not included in the computation of  2004 diluted EPS because the effect would be anti-dilutive</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">Convertible debt instruments, including convertible interest, which  would result in the issuance of 5,303,925, 5,467,769 and, 5,176,170 shares of  common stock, if the conversion features were exercised, were outstanding  during 2005, 2004 and 2003 respectively, but were not included in the  computation of the 2005, 2004 or 2003 diluted EPS because the effect would be  anti-dilutive. The conversion price of these instruments was $7.50 per share at  December 31, 2005, 2004 and 2003 and remained outstanding at December 31, 2005.  </font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman"><b>Note 14 - Major Customers</b></font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">Most of the Company&#146;s business activity is with customers engaged in  drilling and operating natural gas and oil wells primarily in the major onshore  and offshore natural gas and oil producing areas of the U.S., including  offshore in the Gulf of Mexico and onshore in Alabama, Colorado, Louisiana, Mississippi,  Montana, New Mexico, North Dakota, Oklahoma, Texas, Utah, and Wyoming.&#160; Substantially all of the Company&#146;s accounts  receivable at December 31, 2005 and 2004 are from such customers. Performance  in accordance with the credit arrangements is in part dependent upon the  economic condition of the oil and natural gas industry in the respective  geographic areas. The Company does not require its customers to pledge  collateral on their accounts receivable.</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">There were no customers from whom the Company earned in excess of 10%  of its revenues during the years ended December 31, 2005, 2004 or 2003.</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman"><b>Note 15 - Stock Options</b></font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">The 2000 Stock Incentive Plan (&#147;2000 Incentive Plan&#148;) provides for the  granting of incentive stock options or non-qualified stock options to purchase  shares of the Company&#146;s common stock to key employees and non-employee  directors or consultants.&#160; The 2000  Incentive Plan authorizes the issuance of options to purchase up to an  aggregate of 1,750,000 shares of common stock with maximum option terms of ten  years from the date of the grant.&#160; There  are five types of grants that can be made under the 2000 Incentive Plan. The  Discretionary Option Grant Program allows eligible individuals in the Company&#146;s  employ or service (including officers and consultants) to be granted options to  purchase shares of common stock at an exercise price equal to not less than the  fair market value of the stock at the date of the grant.&#160; All grants made in 2000 were made under this  program.&#160; The Stock Issuance Program is  a
non-compensatory program under which individuals in the Company&#146;s employ or  service may be issued shares of common stock directly through the purchase of  such shares at a price not less than the fair market value at the time of  issuance or as a bonus tied to performance.&#160;  The Salary Investment Option Grant Program is a compensatory program  that, if activated by the plan administrator, will allow executive officers and  other highly compensated employees the opportunity to apply a portion of their  base salary to the acquisition of special below market stock grants.&#160; The Automatic Option Grant Program causes  options to be granted automatically at periodic intervals to eligible  non-employee members of the Board of Directors to purchase shares of common stock  at an exercise price equal to their fair market value at the date of the  grant.&#160; The Director Fee Option Grant  Program is a compensatory program that, if activated by the plan administrator,  would allow non-employee
Board members the opportunity to apply a portion of  any annual retainer fee otherwise payable to them in cash each year to the  acquisition of special below market option grants.&#160; </font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">The Board and shareholders approved the 2000 Incentive Plan on February  11, 2000 and an amendment on February 9, 2001, respectively.&#160; At December 31, 2005, 1,954,250 shares had  been granted, of which 902,000 shares were cancelled and 697,750 remained to be  granted under this plan.</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">The 1997 Omnibus Incentive Plan (&#147;1997 Omnibus Plan&#148;) provides for the  granting of either incentive stock options or nonqualified stock options to  purchase shares of the Company&#146;s common stock to key employees responsible for  the direction and management of the Company. The 1997 Omnibus Plan authorizes  the issuance of options to purchase up to an aggregate of 60,000 shares of  common stock, with maximum option terms of ten years from the date of grant.  During 1998, the Board authorized an amendment to the 1997 Omnibus Plan to  allow additional issuances of options to purchase 40,000 shares of common  stock. This amendment increases the total aggregate number of shares under the  1997 Omnibus Plan to 100,000.&#160; The  amendment was approved by the shareholders on February 9, 2001.&#160; At December 31, 2005 and 2004, 7,530 options  were outstanding.&#160; At December 31, 2005,  92,470 options remain available to be granted.&#160;  Options
to purchase 35,520 shares of common stock were cancelled during  2004 and no options were cancelled during 2005.</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">The 1997 Non-Employee Stock Option Plan (&#147;1997 Non-Employee Plan&#148;)  provides for the granting of nonqualified stock options to purchase shares of  the Company&#146;s common stock to non-employee directors and consultants. The 1997  Non-Employee Plan authorizes the issuance of options to purchase up to an  aggregate of 10,000 shares of common stock, with maximum option terms of ten  years from the date of grant. During 1998, the Board authorized an amendment to  the 1997 Non-Employee Plan to allow additional issuances of options to purchase  20,000 shares of common stock. This amendment increases the total aggregate  number of shares under the 1997 Non-Employee Plan to 30,000. &#160;The amendment was approved by the  shareholders on February 9, 2001.&#160; At  December 31, 2005 and 2004, no options were outstanding, respectively.&#160; At December 31, 2005, 30,000 options remain  available to be granted.&#160; Pertinent  information regarding stock
options is as follows:</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman"><b>Note 16  - Contingencies</b></font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">The Company is the subject of various legal actions in the ordinary  course of business. Management does not believe the ultimate outcome of these  actions will have a materially adverse effect on the financial position,  results of operations or cash flows of the Company. </font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">In March, 2006, one of the Company&#146;s shareholders presented it with a  demand for corrective action to remedy alleged breaches of fiduciary duty by  William L. Jenkins, Charles E. Underbrink and James H. Harrison.&#160; The shareholder alleges that these directors  breached their fiduciary duties in connection with various transactions, including  the exchange of the Company&#146;s warrants for shares of its common stock in  October and November 2005, the extension of the expiration date of the  Company&#146;s warrants in December 2004, the Company&#146;s failure to refinance certain  of its derivative securities by the end of 2004, the amendment of the Company&#146;s  certificate of incorporation in December 2005 and the triggering of the change  of control payment due to Mr. Jenkins in December 2005.&#160; The shareholder further alleges that these  directors were interested in such transactions, that such transactions were not  fair to the Company and
that the St. James Partnerships, Simmons &amp; Company  International, Ron E. Whitter and another officer of the company participated  in such breaches and/or aided and abetted them. &#160;The shareholder has indicated that if the Company fails to take  appropriate action to remedy the breaches following the presentation of its  demand, it intends to bring a derivative suit on behalf of the Company.&#160; The Company&#146;s board of directors intends to  take such steps as it considers appropriate to investigate this matter.&#160; However, based on information received  through March 23, 2006, the Company believes these allegations are without  merit and, if a suit is filed, the Company expects that it will be vigorously  defended.&#160; The Company does not expect  the liability, if any, resulting from this matter to have a material adverse  effect on its current financial position, results of operations or cash flows.</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">The St. James Partnerships, their
general partners and Charles E. Underbrink, who is a Director of the Company and
a director of the general partners of the St. James Partnerships were added as
defendants in an amended complaint filed in March 2005 in Texas by two of the
limited partners of the St. James Partnerships.&#160; The action was originally
instituted in December 2004 against the auditors of the St. James Partnerships.
The plaintiffs brought the action as a class action on behalf of all the limited
partners of the St. James Partnerships and are seeking class action
certification.&#160; No claim has been asserted against the Company and the
Company is not a defendant in the action.&#160; However, the complaint and the
amended complaint in the action contain allegations that the Company
participated with Mr. Underbrink in actions the plaintiffs allege were
fraudulent and constituted securities violations.&#160; The</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></div>

<div  align="center"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">F-35</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman"><b>Note 17  - Fair Value of Financial Instruments</b></font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">The following methods and assumptions were used to estimate the fair  value of each class of financial instruments for which it is practicable to  estimate fair value:</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman"><b>Cash and  Cash Equivalents, Restricted Cash, Accounts Receivable, Current Portion of  Long-Term Debt and Accounts Payable</b> - The carrying amount is  a reasonable estimate of the fair value because of the short maturity of these  instruments.</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman"><b>Long-Term  Debt</b> - The carrying value of the Company&#146;s long-term debt  approximates fair value due to the variable nature of the interest rate and the  interest rate reset periods.</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman"><b>Related Party Debt</b>  - Management is unable to estimate the fair value of the Company&#146;s related  party debt.&#160; This debt is due in 2009  but is subject to subordination to the Company&#146;s senior debt. The debt and  accumulated accrued interest in aggregate is carried at a book value of $40.1  million in the statement of financial position at December 31, 2005.&#160; This debt is convertible at a conversion  price of $7.50 per share, which is significantly below the market price of the  Company&#146;s common stock at December 31, 2005, and it is significantly below the  Company&#146;s expectations for the price per share to be received in the planned  public equity offering.&#160; While the  Company is unable to estimate the fair value of its related party debt, the  Company reasonably believes it exceeds the book value because of its  convertibility.</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman"><b>Note 18 -  Employee Benefit Plan</b></font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">The Company maintains a Retirement Savings  Plan (the 401(k) Plan) for its employees, which allows participants to make  contributions by salary reduction pursuant to Section 401(k) of the Internal  Revenue Code.&#160; The Company&#146;s contributions  to the 401(k) Plan are discretionary.&#160;  Employees vest in their contributions immediately and vest in the  Company&#146;s contributions ratably over six years.&#160; The Company made no contributions to the 401(k) Plan for the  years ended December 31, 2005, 2004, and 2003.</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman"><b>Note 19 - Segment and Related Information</b></font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">With the acquisition of Bobcat, the Company currently conducts its  business through two operating segments as described below.&#160; The Company included operating results from  its acquisition of Bobcat subsequent to its acquisition on December 16, 2005:</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman"><i>Wireline  Segment.</i>&#160; The  Company&#146;s wireline segment, which accounted for 99.0% of its revenues for the  year ended December 31, 2005, operated a fleet of 51 cased-hole wireline trucks  and 15 offshore wireline skids and three P&amp;A packages as of  December&nbsp;31, 2005.&#160; All of the  Company&#146;s wireline trucks and offshore skids are equipped with top-of-the-line  computer systems.&#160; The Company primarily  provides services in cased-hole environments.&#160;  Cased-hole wireline services are performed during and after the  completion of the well, and from time to time thereafter during the life of the  well.&#160; Wireline services are performed  using a wire cable that is lowered from a truck or skid into a well with  various types of tools and instruments attached to the end of the cable.&#160; Once in the well, the instruments can  transmit data back to a computer system in the truck or skid for analysis.&#160; Specific
wireline services include: logging  services such as cement bond evaluation, production logging and other  measurements; pipe recovery services; and perforating and mechanical services  such as setting plugs and packers.&#160;  Other services in the wireline segment include plug and abandonment (&#147;P&amp;A&#148;)  services, which are used at the end of a well&#146;s productive life, and tubing  conveyed perforating (&#147;TCP&#148;), which is a method of perforating the casing in  order to open the flow path in a well for hydrocarbons.&#160; The Company operates four P&amp;A packages  in connection with its P&amp;A services.</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman"><i>Well  Intervention Segment.</i>&#160;  The Company&#146;s well intervention segment accounted for 1% of revenues for  the year ended December 31, 2005. The Company included well intervention  revenues from the date of acquisition on December 16, 2005 only.&#160; The Company operated a fleet of 14 snubbing  units as of December 31, 2005.&#160; The  </font></div>

<div><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></div>

<div  align="center"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">F-36</font></div>

<div  align="center"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;</font></div>

  <div>
    <hr noshade size="1">

</div>

<div>
  <p><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;Company primarily provides snubbing services utilizing specialized high pressure snubbing equipment that allows an operator to service a well without using other more disruptive means to control the pressure in the well.&#160; The Company&#146;s well intervention segment also includes other related oil field services, such as freezing services, hot tapping services, rental tools and fishing services.&#160; </font></p>
